This is standard hypothesis-class containment with the source strictly more general, so the direction is correct. Historically this was indeed the recognized route; the planar case was resolved by Dujmović, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt, Wood (2019) via the closely related graph product structure theorem.

If no O(n^{2-eps}) algorithm for map isomorphism exists for any eps > 0 (source), then in particular no O(n polylog n) algorithm exists, since n polylog n = O(n^{1.5}) = O(n^{2-1/2}). Thus the truth of the source's quadratic lower bound conjecture entails the truly-superlinear lower bound for map isomorphism that the target subproblem asks to establish — indeed unconditionally, which is stronger than the conditional bound sought. Caveat: the target is an informal call to prove such a bound rather than a crisp proposition; read as the proposition 'a truly superlinear lower bound holds for map isomorphism', the implication is elementary and the direction (source stronger) is correct.

The full text of arXiv:2009.03418 (Conjecture 5) states cr(M_{n,t}) = H(n) - (1/2)t(k-1)(k-2) for n >= 5 and 0 <= t <= n/2, explicitly including t = 0. Since M_{n,0} = K_n and the correction term vanishes at t = 0, the conjecture's t = 0 instance reads cr(K_n) = H(n), which is exactly the Harary-Hill conjecture (the cases n < 5 are trivially known, cr = 0). So truth of the M_{n,t} conjecture for all admissible (n,t) forces the Harary-Hill value for all n: a clean instance-restriction implication in the claimed direction.

Every outerplanar graph is planar, so the class in the target is contained in the class in the source. By Theorem 3 of the same paper (quoted in the target's context), outerplanar graphs have cop number at most 2, so on the outerplanar subclass only the values 1 and 2 occur. Hence a classification of planar graphs by cop number i in {1,2,3}, restricted to outerplanar graphs, is precisely the 1-cop-win vs 2-cop-win classification asked in the target. Solving the source problem solves the target: a rigorous hypothesis-class restriction in the claimed direction.

Maximum Independent Set is the special case of Maximum Weight Independent Set with all weights equal to 1, on the same graph class (perfect graphs). Specializing weights to 1 preserves both polynomial running time and the combinatorial (non-ellipsoid) character of an algorithm, so a combinatorial polynomial-time MWIS algorithm for perfect graphs is in particular a combinatorial polynomial-time (hence also FPT) MIS algorithm for perfect graphs, answering the target. The converse specialization is not automatic (weighted is a priori harder), so 'implies' rather than 'equivalent_to' is the right relation, in the claimed direction.

MIS is the unit-weight special case of MWIS on the same class (even-hole-free graphs). A positive answer to the source question — a polynomial-time algorithm for MWIS on even-hole-free graphs — immediately yields a polynomial-time algorithm for MIS on even-hole-free graphs by setting all weights to 1, which settles the target's open complexity question (placing it in P). The direction is correct: the weighted problem is the stronger statement; a resolution of the unweighted question would not by itself resolve the weighted one.

The dichotomy conjecture's 'if' direction asserts MIS is in P on H-free graphs for every H that is a path P_l or a subdivided claw S_{i,j,k}. Every H in the target (an S_{i,j,k} containing P7, S_{1,1,3}, or S_{1,2,2}) belongs to that family by hypothesis, so truth of the conjecture answers the target completely: MIS is polynomial for all such H-free classes. The direction is correct — the source is the stronger, universally quantified statement; the target asks only about a boundary subfamily of spiders. This is a direct instantiation, no subtle parameter mismatch.

Monotonicity of parameters gives the containment: every induced odd cycle packing is an induced cycle packing, so iocp(G) <= icp(G) for all G. An O_k-free graph has icp(G) <= k-1, hence iocp(G) <= k-1, so O_k-free graphs form a subclass of graphs with bounded iocp. Thus a polynomial algorithm for MIS on bounded-iocp graphs restricts to O_k-free graphs, proving the target conjecture. The paper's own context confirms the direction, calling bounded-iocp tractability 'a formidable generalisation of Conjecture 1.3' (the target). Minor caveat: the source statement says 'tractable' informally, but under the natural polynomial-time reading the implication is rigorous.

The source's explicit 'in particular' clause asserts polynomial-time stable set for ALL graphs with ocp(G) <= k, for every fixed k. Since every finite graph embeds in a surface of some Euler genus, 'graphs of arbitrary Euler genus with ocp <= k' is exactly the class of all graphs with ocp <= k; the target is therefore an instance (indeed a restatement) of the source's second clause, and the full source is strictly stronger since it also asserts polynomial solvability of all bounded sub-determinant IPs. Hypothesis-class containment is trivial and the direction is correct.

Any witness for iocp(G) >= t (pairwise vertex-disjoint, pairwise-anticomplete induced odd cycles) is in particular a family of t vertex-disjoint odd cycles, so iocp(G) <= ocp(G) for every graph G. Hence the class {G : ocp(G) <= k} is contained in {G : iocp(G) <= k}, and the target's extra hypothesis (embeddability in some surface) only shrinks it further. Polynomial tractability of MIS on bounded-iocp graphs (source) therefore yields it on bounded-ocp graphs of arbitrary genus (target). The source's own context confirms the direction: it calls bounded-iocp tractability 'a formidable generalisation ... of the known polynomial-time result for bounded ocp'. Direction as claimed.

The source asks, for every k >= 3, for a complete characterisation of the graphs H for which k-Coloring on H-free graphs is polynomial vs NP-hard. The target concerns k = 5 and a specific family of forbidden graphs H (one component P4, the rest an induced subgraph of rP3 containing an edge). Each such (k=5, H) pair is an instance of the source's classification, so resolving the source dichotomy for k = 5 in particular determines the complexity of every case in the target family. Pure instantiation/restriction; direction as claimed (source is the stronger, universal statement).

The five remaining open pairs for boundedness of clique-width of (H1,H2)-free graphs are enumerated in the companion survey by Dabrowski, Johnson and Paulusma (arXiv:1901.00335, Open Problem 4.20): H1 = K3 with H2 in {P1+S_{1,1,3}, S_{1,2,3}}; H1 = diamond with H2 in {P1+P2+P3, P1+P5}; H1 = gem with H2 = P2+P3. The pair (K3, S_{1,2,3}) is item (i), so the target question ('do (triangle, S_{1,2,3})-free graphs have bounded clique-width?') is exactly one of the five cases the source asks to determine. Resolving all five (source) in particular answers the target. Direction as claimed.

Hypothesis-class containment holds with a parameter shift: a semi-induced half-graph H_{2t,2t} (a_i~b_j iff i<=j) contains K_{t,t} as a subgraph (take a_1..a_t against b_{t+1}..b_{2t}; all pairs satisfy i<=j), so any K_{t,t}-subgraph-free graph is H_{2t,2t}-free. Hence an FPT algorithm for Grundy Coloring on H_{t,t}-free graphs for all t applies to K_{t,t}-free graphs via t'=2t. The paper itself states the containment: 'excluding a K_{t,t} implies excluding a large half-graph H_{t,t} (but not vice versa)', confirming H_{t,t}-free is the larger class and the source the stronger question. Direction as claimed is correct.

Instance-of-general relation, both questions from the same paper: the target asks, for a given class G, whether a constant c_G bounds gamma/rho over G; the source asks to characterize exactly the classes for which such a constant exists. Any resolution of the characterization answers the per-class question for each given class, so the source is the stronger problem and solving it solves the target. Direction as claimed is correct. Arguably near-equivalent phrasings (answering every instance constitutes an extensional characterization), but the claimed implication certainly holds.

Valid restriction to bidirected inputs: Sigma-k-DICOLOURABILITY takes 'a digraph D embeddable on Sigma' (digons allowed), and the paper explicitly uses chi(G) = dichromatic number of the bidirected graph of G to derive NP-completeness of Sigma-3-DICOLOURABILITY from 3-colourability on Sigma. For G embeddable on Sigma, its bidirected digraph embeds on Sigma and is 4-dicolourable iff G is 4-colourable (colour classes must avoid digons, i.e., be independent). So a poly-time algorithm for Sigma-4-DICOLOURABILITY (positive resolution of the source, k=4) answers the target. Caveat: an NP-completeness resolution of the source would not settle the target; conversely NP-hardness of the target transfers to the source, as the target is a special case.

Rigorous by induction on nu. Base: nu=0 means no edges, tau=0. Step: the source conjecture gives k in [1,r-1] and a set S of k(r-1) vertices with nu(H-S) <= nu-k (necessarily k <= nu, since nu cannot drop by more than nu). H-S is still r-partite r-uniform, so by induction tau(H-S) <= (r-1)(nu-k); the cover of H-S together with S covers H, of size <= (r-1)(nu-k)+k(r-1) = (r-1)nu, i.e. tau <= (r-1)nu, which is Ryser's conjecture. Direction correct: the deletion conjecture is the stronger statement. The source's own context also states it is 'a weakening of Lovász's conjecture that still implies Ryser's conjecture'.

Recovered the truncated statement from the paper's PDF: Conjecture 6.2 reads 'There is a constant c_k>0 such that for every k-uniform k-partite hypergraph H, ex(n,H) <= O_H(n^{k-c_k/d_max(H)})'. For a d x d Latin square, d_1(H_L), d_2(H_L) = Theta(d), so d_max(H_L)=Theta(d) and 6.2 gives the upper bound ex(n,H_L) <= n^{3-Omega(1/d)}. The matching lower bound ex(n,H_L) >= Omega(n^{3-C/d}) is unconditional from the paper's proven Theorem 1.4 (lower bound Omega_k(n^{k-C_k/d_1(H)}) with d_1(H_L)=Theta(d)). Together: ex(n,H_L)=n^{3-Theta(1/d)}, exactly Conjecture 6.4. The paper itself presents H_L as a test case of 6.2 ('matching d_max(H_L)=Theta(d) via Conjecture 6.2'). Implication uses only the conjecture plus the paper's proven theorem; direction correct.

The sketch's first step is rigorous: orbit-averaging (sum_gamma |B ∩ gammaB| = |B|^2|Gamma|/n >= |Gamma|) forces |B| >= sqrt(n) for every generator. But the counting step is a genuine open gap: a set-intersecting A has |A| = k^n * mu_{1/k}(up(B)) with up(B) a symmetric intersecting upset of sets, and proving mu_{1/k} <= exp(-c n^delta) for all such families is itself open (known Ellis-Kalai-Narayanan-type bounds decay only roughly polynomially in n). Logically the source could hold while the target fails. Supporting evidence: the paper's phrasing 'Failing that, it would be very interesting to at least show [the target]' treats the source as the stronger goal, and the best set-intersecting construction (projective-plane lines) has size ~k^{n-sqrt(n)}, consistent with delta=1/2. Missing: a proof that all set-intersecting families are <= k^{n-cn^delta}.

A 57-regular Moore graph of diameter 2 and girth 5 has 3250 vertices and is strongly regular with parameters (3250,57,0,1): girth 5 forces lambda=0 (triangle-free) and diameter 2 with girth 5 forces mu=1. None of the seven known triangle-free strongly regular graphs (C5, Petersen, Clebsch, Hoffman-Singleton, Gewirtz, the (77,16,0,4) graph, Higman-Sims) has these parameters, so its existence yields an eighth, answering the target affirmatively. The target's OPG context states this implication verbatim: 'Every Moore Graph of diameter 2 is a triangle-free strongly regular graph, so if there is a 57-regular Moore graph of diameter 2, this would add another to the list.' Direction correct.

The paper (per both contexts) proves the reduction: non-semisimple finite R yields non-prime X_R, and for semisimple R = prod F_{q_i} one has X_R ≅ prod K_{q_i}. Hence Q4.28 (when is X_R prime?) is settled by answering Q4.31 (when is prod K_{n_i} prime?) restricted to prime-power n_i — a special case of the source question, which allows arbitrary positive integers. Answering the source thus answers the target; direction correct (general combinatorial question is stronger). Note this is an answer-to-answer implication between Questions, resting on the paper's already-proven reduction stated in the provided context.

Hypothesis-class containment: intersecting winning families are among the balanced monotone families, giving the pointwise inequality p_monotone(t) ≥ p_intersecting(t) ≥ p_dict(t), which the paper states explicitly (both contexts). If the larger quantity p_monotone(t) tends to 0, the sandwiched nonnegative quantity p_intersecting(t) must also tend to 0. Direction correct: Conjecture 2.2 (monotone) is the stronger statement, as the paper itself says ('progressively stronger').

The target's context states the exact identity p_intersecting(t,n) = ᾱ(K(n)^{□t}) (Kneser graph on {0,1}^n, Hamming product) and explicitly describes Conjecture 2.6 as 'a graph-theoretic restatement of Conjecture 2.1'. Under this identity, p_intersecting(t) → 0 is the same assertion as lim_t lim_n ᾱ(K(n)^{□t}) = 0, so the two conjectures are equivalent, not merely one-way. Minor caveat: the batch text does not show how p_intersecting(t) absorbs the n-parameter (presumably lim or sup over n), but the paper's own declaration of restatement resolves this.

The source's context states explicitly: 'This conjecture would imply Conjecture 2.6 and hence Levine's conjecture.' The mechanism is coherent: ε*(α) > 0 for all α ∈ (0,1/2) gives a uniform gap ᾱ(G) − α*(G) ≥ ε*(α) over every graph with ᾱ(G) ≥ α, and applying this uniformly along the Hamming powers K(n)^{□t} forces the fractional independence to decrease by a fixed amount at each power, driving the double limit to 0. Only an implication is claimed (2.8 is the stronger, more general statement about all graphs); no reverse direction is asserted. Direction as claimed is correct.

Hypothesis-class containment. The target's context states verbatim that ε**>0 'is the special case of Conjecture 2.8 where the random-subset distribution is simply binomial'. The binomial distribution (each vertex independently Bernoulli(1/2)) is a member of the class of positively-correlated random-subset distributions with Bernoulli(1/2) marginals used to define α*(G): independence is the trivial case of positive correlation. Hence α**(G) is the binomial instance of the quantity entering α*(G), and a uniform gap ε*(α)>0 for the optimal/general distribution in the class yields the same gap ε**(α) ≥ ε*(α) > 0 for the binomial instance. Direction is correct: the general-class statement (source) is the stronger one.

Explicitly stated and proved in the paper (Conlon–Fox–Grinshpun–He, 'Online Ramsey numbers and the subgraph query problem'). The paper writes: 'Assume Conjecture 9..., i.e., f(K_m,p)=2^{o(m)}p^{-2m/3+c_m} for all m≥3, p∈(0,1). By Theorem 10, we have r̃(m,n;p)=Θ(min{f(K_m,p), f(K_n,1−p)})', and optimizing over p yields both parts of Conjecture 7 (the target). Since Theorem 10 is a proven result, the truth of Conjecture 9 (source) alone forces the target's growth rates 2^{(2/3+o(1))n} and n^{(2/3+o(1))m}. Direction as claimed: source is the stronger statement.

Explicitly stated in the paper. In the arXiv TeX source of 2211.01032, Section 9 (Open Problems) states, immediately after the target conjecture ('For any p(n): N→[0,1], almost all graphs in G(n,p) satisfy E[F]=O(log n)'): 'This conjecture would follow from the stronger statement of Conjecture \ref{con:random}.' I verified that con:random is exactly the source statement (Conjecture 1.13: E[F]=(1+o(1))ln(pn^2) for a random embedding of G∈G(n,p)). Mathematically the route is ln(pn^2) ≤ 2 ln n for all p ≤ 1, combined with the Markov-inequality argument the authors use in Corollary 7.3 to pass from the expectation over (graph, embedding) to almost all graphs. Direction as claimed: source is the stronger statement.

I recovered the truncated Question from the paper's PDF: 'Determine when G(n,p) is 2-reconstructible. Is there a threshold around n^{-3/4} (up to a polylogarithmic factor)?' — it concerns only r=2 (the sole Question environment in the paper; r=1 gets no Question), not r in {1,2} as the ingested record guessed. The source, instantiated at r=2, asserts existence of a sharp second threshold t(n) for 2-reconstructibility, which answers the qualitative existence part of the Question; but it says nothing about the threshold's location, so it neither 'determines when' nor confirms the specific guess n^{-3/4}. The restriction implication thus covers only part of the target's content, and the target as ingested was truncated, so I cap the verdict at plausible. Direction (general statement -> r=2 instance) is as claimed.

The implication is explicitly stated in the paper's own text (quoted in the source context): the truth of Conjecture 3.1 'would imply, by a simple inductive argument, that f(n) = 2n-2 for all n >= 2'. The mechanism is standard: the conjectured bipartition [n] = P ∪ Q with two circle intervals lets one split the n agents into two groups, each satisfied on its own interval, and recurse, yielding f(n) <= 2n-2; the matching lower bound f(n) >= 2n-2 is already a theorem via the Segal-Halevi construction, so the conjecture forces the exact equality f(n) = 2n-2, which is precisely the target statement. Direction as claimed: source (Conjecture 3.1) is the stronger topological statement, target is the numerical consequence.

The implication is explicitly stated in the target's context: 'Conjecture 4 follows from Conjecture 3, since vec-t(n) >= n/vec-a(n)'. The arithmetic checks out: Conjecture 3's upper-bound half vec-a(n) = O(sqrt(n log n)) plugged into the standard inequality dichromatic number >= n / (max acyclic set size) gives the missing lower bound vec-t(n) = Omega(sqrt(n/log n)); the matching upper bound vec-t(n) <= (sqrt(2)+o(1)) sqrt(n/log n) is already proved in the same paper, so vec-t(n) = Theta(sqrt(n/log n)) follows, which is exactly Conjecture 4. Direction as claimed: the acyclic-number conjecture (source) is the stronger statement implying the dichromatic-number conjecture (target).

Verified in both PDFs (companion papers by the same four authors). In 2208.06629, U_t(n) is the minimum number of lazy transpositions in a (t,n)-shuffle, i.e. achieving t-uniformity on n points, and Problem 3 asks 'Does U_t(n) = tn - binom(t+1,2)?'. In 2208.06630, a 2-uniformity network is defined identically and Conjecture 1 states the minimum is 2n-3 = 2n - binom(3,2), exactly the t=2 instance of Problem 3's formula. An affirmative answer to the general problem at t=2 (t=n is already refuted by Theorem 2) is literally the target conjecture: implication by restriction. The DMTCS version of 2208.06630 footnotes that Conjecture 1 was later proven by Janzer, Johnson, Leader (2023), corroborating that the two quantities coincide.
citations: B. Janzer, J. R. Johnson, I. Leader. Partial shuffles by lazy swaps. SIAM J. Discrete Math., 37(4):2544-2557, 2023.

edges.argument: Elementary set-theoretic containment: if there exists k0 such that F is k-nice for every k >= k0, then the set {k : F is k-nice} contains the infinite set {k0, k0+1, ...}, so F is k-nice for infinitely many k. Both statements quantify over the same hypothesis class (finite families containing at least one forest) with the same notion of k-nice, from the same paper. The target's own context text explicitly states it is 'posed as a weaker version of Question 1.1', confirming the direction: source (for-all-large k) is stronger, target (infinitely many k) is weaker.

Hypothesis-class containment. For a fixed surface S, the class C_S of graphs embeddable in S is minor-closed (deleting/contracting edges cannot increase genus, i.e. genus is minor-monotone) and proper (K_n for large n does not embed in S, since the genus of K_n grows unboundedly). Hence any connected graph embedded in a fixed surface lies in a proper minor-closed family, and the source conjecture's conclusion xc(P_sp.trees(G)) = O(|V|) applies to it, which is exactly the target's conclusion. Direction is correct: the minor-closed conjecture (Conjecture 2 in the paper) is the stronger, more general statement and restricts to the bounded-genus conjecture (Conjecture 1).

The intended relation is right: the source conjecture (an analogue of Theorem 1.14 for arbitrary Z-coefficient patterns over arbitrary abelian groups) would, if true, answer the target problem affirmatively, since arbitrary abelian groups include F_q^n and Z, and arbitrary patterns include those of complexity greater than 1 (integer coefficients acting on F_q^n cover F_q-coefficient patterns after reduction mod q). However, the source is explicitly informal: the authors 'decline to give a precise formulation due to unresolved issues with infinite complexity and trivial solutions', and those caveats could exclude cases the target problem asks about (e.g. infinite-complexity patterns over Z). Without a precise source statement one cannot rigorously certify the implication, so this stays at plausible rather than confirmed.

Subproblem containment between two questions from the same paper. Part (iii) of Problem 1.2 asks for the order of magnitude of f(d)/f_{<=2}(d) and in particular whether it is exponential in n = 2^{d-1}; the target Question asks precisely whether f(d)/f_{<=2}(d) is subexponential in n. Any resolution of Problem 1.2's part (iii) — determining the growth rate of that ratio — immediately answers the subexponentiality question. The target's own context states it 'addresses Problem 1.2 (iii)'. Since these are problems rather than truth-valued conjectures, 'implies' is read as: a solution to the source yields a solution to the target, which holds by restriction to ratio (iii).

The source's own statement records the implication: the lamination conjecture, combined with the lower bound n(2,d) > (1-o(1))d^2/2 which is already PROVED in the same paper (Theorem 2), yields lim n(2,d)/d^2 = 1/2. Since the lower bound is a theorem, the conjecture alone forces the limit to exist and equal 1/2, which in particular answers the target question ('does the limit exist?') affirmatively. Direction is correct: source (conjecture, giving the value 1/2) is strictly stronger than target (mere existence of the limit). Same paper, same quantity n(2,d), no parameter mismatch.

The source conjecture asserts T(G) = Theta-tilde(sqrt(|G|)) for ALL finite groups G, hence in particular T(p) = Theta-tilde(sqrt(p)) for cyclic groups of prime order. This settles both parts of the target question: (i) the behavior of T(n) at primes is not different from composite n beyond polylogarithmic factors (in particular the current subgroup-based O(p^{3/4+eps}) bound is far from tight), and (ii) T(G) depends on the structure of G, beyond |G|, only up to polylog factors, since sqrt(|G|) is determined by the order alone. Hypothesis class containment is immediate (primes/arbitrary groups are subcases of the universally quantified conjecture). Direction correct: conjecture is the stronger statement. Only residual imprecision: the question's 'how much' is answered only up to the polylog slack built into Theta-tilde, which is exactly the resolution the paper intends.

A positive answer to the source (cop number <= f(genus)) bounds the target supremum. Cut locus at distance >= 1 means injectivity radius >= 1, hence systole >= 2. Gromov's systolic inequality for closed surfaces of genus g >= 2 gives sys^2 <= C (log g)^2/g * area, so area <= alpha and sys >= 2 force g/(log g)^2 <= C*alpha/4, i.e. genus <= G(alpha) finite; genus 0 and 1 are trivially included. Then the sup over the class is <= max_{g <= G(alpha)} f(g) < infinity, answering 'Is it bounded?' affirmatively. Direction correct: the source bounds cop number over ALL metrics of each genus, which is exactly what controls the target class (bounded genus, varying metric). Standard argument; only caveat is the informal 'cut locus at least 1', which the target's context confirms means an injectivity radius lower bound.
citations: M. Gromov, Filling Riemannian manifolds, J. Differential Geom. 18 (1983), 1-147 (systolic inequality for surfaces)

edges.argument: The implication is explicitly stated in the source's own OPG context: 'for k=2, Jaeger showed that this conjecture (if true) would imply the 5-flow conjecture.' The full modular orientation conjecture (all k) contains the k=2 case (every 8-edge-connected graph has a modular 5-orientation, equivalently a 5/2-flow), and Jaeger's reduction derives nowhere-zero 5-flows for all bridgeless graphs from it, so truth of the source forces truth of the target. Direction correct. Note the source conjecture has since been disproved (for k >= 3, by Han, Li, Wu, Zhang), but that does not affect the validity of the conditional implication, and the k=2 case relevant to the reduction remains open.
citations: F. Jaeger, On circular flows in graphs, in: Finite and Infinite Sets (Eger, 1981), Colloq. Math. Soc. Janos Bolyai 37, North-Holland, 1984, 391-402

edges.argument: Confirmed, after correcting both extracted statements. Verbatim Conjecture 2 of 2308.15721: 'χ⋆(G_H^odd) ≤ 2·td̄(H)−2 and χ_Δ(G_H^odd) = td̄(H)−1' (the batch's 'χ⋆ = td̄(H)−1' is a mis-extraction). NSSW's Conjecture 4 in 1708.02370 reads 'χ⋆(M_H) ≤ 2 td(H)−2' where their td denotes CONNECTED tree-depth ('We choose to work with connected tree-depth to avoid this distinction'), i.e. td̄ in the odd-minor paper's notation. An odd H-minor is in particular an H-minor, so M_H ⊆ G_H^odd, and χ⋆ is monotone under class containment; hence Conjecture 2 gives χ⋆(M_H) ≤ χ⋆(G_H^odd) ≤ 2td̄(H)−2, exactly the target. Even under the batch's face-value source statement the chain td̄(H)−1 ≤ td(H) ≤ 2td(H)−2 (td ≥ 2, using td̄ ≤ td+1) yields the target. Direction as claimed: odd-minor-free is the larger class, so the source is stronger.

Self-contained hypothesis-strength argument. Source: for every forest H, the class of H-free graphs is polynomially χ-bounded. Polynomial χ-boundedness trivially implies χ-boundedness, so the source implies the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, which is precisely the 'if' direction of the target. The 'only if' direction of the target is a known theorem, not a conjecture: if H contains a cycle, Erdős's construction of graphs with girth > |V(H)| and unbounded chromatic number lies in Forb(H) (these graphs contain no induced H), so Forb(H) is not χ-bounded — the target's own context states this and that the target is equivalent to Gyárfás–Sumner. Hence source ⇒ Gyárfás–Sumner ⇒ target. The converse fails (χ-bounded does not give polynomial bounds), so 'implies' with source strictly stronger is the correct direction.

Self-contained and explicitly stated in the target's context. Suppose every forest H is good: χ(G) ≤ f_H(ω(G)) for H-free G with f_H a polynomial. If G is H-free with no K_d(t) subgraph, then ω(G) < dt, since a clique on dt vertices contains the complete d-partite graph K_d(t) as a spanning subgraph. Hence χ(G) ≤ f_H(dt), which for fixed d is a polynomial in t — exactly the definition of H being multibounding. So the source implies every forest is multibounding. The target's context confirms this: 'any forest satisfying the polynomial-bound Conjecture 1.2 is multibounding.' The converse is not known (2303.11766 proves paths and brooms are multibounding while polynomial χ-boundedness even for P5 remains open), so the direction 'source implies target' is correct and strict.

Assume Hoàng-Reed for k=r on an n-vertex digraph with min outdegree r: it yields cycles C_1,...,C_r where each C_j meets the union of the earlier ones in at most one vertex. Hence |C_1 ∪ ... ∪ C_r| >= sum_i |C_i| - (r-1), and this union has at most n vertices, so sum_i |C_i| <= n + r - 1. The shortest C_i then has length at most floor((n+r-1)/r) = ceil(n/r), which is exactly Caccetta-Häggkvist. The implication is also explicitly stated in both provided contexts (Hoàng-Reed page: 'This conjecture would imply the Caccetta-Häggkvist Conjecture'; C-H page lists Hoàng-Reed as implying it). Direction as claimed.

Hypothesis-class containment: delta^0(D) = min(min-outdegree, min-indegree), so any digraph with delta^0(D) >= f(k) in particular has minimum outdegree >= f(k). If Mader's outdegree conjecture holds with f(k), every such digraph contains a TT_k subdivision, so mader_{delta^0}(TT_k) exists and is <= f(k). The semidegree hypothesis is the stronger assumption, making the outdegree conjecture the stronger statement; direction as claimed. The target's own context notes the paper proves the two are in fact equivalent (via mader_{delta^+}(TT_k) <= mader_{delta^0}(TT_{2k})), but the claimed one-way implication is immediate from the statements alone.

The source's own context states the implication explicitly: given a 1/2-flow-pair (phi_2, phi_4), the combination (5*phi_2 + phi_4)/2 is a circular 5-flow. Checking: if phi_2(e) = ±1 then |5*phi_2(e) + phi_4(e)| ∈ [2,8] (since |phi_4(e)| <= 3), so the value lies in [1,4]; if phi_2(e) = 0 the condition |phi_4(e)| >= 2 gives a value in [1, 3/2]. All edge values lie in [1, 5-1] in absolute value, i.e. a circular 5-flow, and by the standard equivalence (Goddyn-Tarsi-Zhang: flow number = ceiling of circular flow number) the graph then has a nowhere-zero 5-flow. Direction as claimed.

The source asserts that for every fixed tree T the class of T-free graphs admits a chi-bounding function polynomial in the clique number; a polynomial chi-bounding function is in particular a chi-bounding function, so the target (Gyárfás-Sumner: T-free graphs are chi-bounded) follows immediately. Strictly stronger statement, same hypothesis class (T-free graphs for every fixed tree T), monotone strengthening of the conclusion only. Direction as claimed. (The source is phrased informally as 'it is possible that...', but read as a conjecture the implication is trivial.)

No implication either way. The 4-flow conjecture concludes NZ 4-flows only for bridgeless graphs with no Petersen minor and says nothing about graphs containing a Petersen minor (e.g. the Petersen graph itself needs a 5-flow), so it cannot yield the 5-flow conjecture. Conversely a NZ 5-flow never gives a NZ 4-flow, so the 5-flow conjecture does not imply the 4-flow conjecture. The cross-mention in the 4-flow page is purely about proof technique: vertex-splitting reduces the 5-flow conjecture to cubic graphs but fails for the 4-flow conjecture because splitting may create a Petersen minor. Both are Tutte flow conjectures, hence thematically linked only.

The connection is flow/local-tension surface duality: as the source page states, Tutte's 5-flow conjecture implies the companion conjecture 'every loopless graph embedded in an ORIENTABLE surface has a 5-local-tension' (local-tensions on G dualize to flows on G*). But the headline 5-local-tensions conjecture (edge-width >= c implies 5-local-tension) ranges over all surfaces; on non-orientable surfaces duality produces flows on BIDIRECTED graphs (Bouchet's setting, parameter 6, not 5), so the 5-flow conjecture covers only the orientable subfamily of the source conjecture. Nor does the source imply the 5-flow conjecture (it is a statement about embedded graphs of large edge-width, not all bridgeless graphs). Subfamily implication only, hence related_only.

Bouchet's conjecture concerns nowhere-zero 6-flows on bidirected graphs, which by duality (as both pages note: 'flows on bidirected graphs arise naturally as duals of local-tensions on a non-orientable surface') implies a 6-LOCAL-TENSION statement for graphs embedded in non-orientable surfaces. The headline source conjecture asks for a 5-local-tension under an edge-width >= c hypothesis; the parameters differ (6 vs 5), so Bouchet's conjecture does not imply it, and the source conjecture, being restricted to large edge-width embeddings and to the number 5, does not imply Bouchet's statement about all bidirected graphs. They are linked by the same duality framework and Bouchet's conjecture is evidence/motivation, but there is no implication in either direction.

Both problems live in the quasi-order defined by cycle-continuous mappings, and the source page's mention of the Petersen coloring conjecture is only to say it is 'the most interesting question on this subject'. The Petersen coloring conjecture (equivalently: every bridgeless graph admits a cycle-continuous map to the Petersen graph) asserts that all bridgeless graphs dominate one fixed element of the order; the antichain problem asks whether the order contains an infinite antichain. Neither statement forces the other: knowing every bridgeless graph maps to Petersen puts no constraint on comparability among arbitrary pairs of graphs, and existence or non-existence of an infinite antichain says nothing about maps to the Petersen graph specifically. Shared framework, no implication.

The OPG page explicitly states and proves that the Addario-Berry et al. conjecture implies Burr's conjecture ONLY for antidirected trees: chi(D) >= 2k-2 yields a colour-critical subdigraph of min degree >= 2k-3, hence arc density > (k-2)|V|, triggering the source conjecture. But Burr's conjecture concerns ALL oriented trees, so the source does not imply the full target (subfamily-only implication). The converse also fails: high arc density does not force high chromatic number (bipartite digraphs with all arcs one way have chi=2 and arbitrary density, as the source context notes). Genuine partial-implication link, but no full implication in either direction, so related_only.

The TCC page states only that the Edge List Coloring Conjecture 'would imply chi''(G) <= Delta(G)+3' (via ch'(G)=chi'(G) <= Delta+1 by Vizing and chi'' <= ch'+2). Delta+3 is strictly weaker than TCC's Delta+2 bound, so ELCC does NOT imply TCC. Conversely TCC, a statement about the total chromatic number, says nothing about list edge colorings, so it does not imply ELCC. The connection is a weak-bound consequence only: the correct classification is related_only, with no implication in either direction.

The mention in the source page is actually to the List Total Colouring Conjecture of Borodin, Kostochka and Woodall, not to Behzad's Total Colouring Conjecture; the match to Behzad's page is a name near-miss. A thematic link survives (total graphs are squares of subdivided graphs, so choosability-of-squares questions bear on total colouring), but there is no implication either way: Noel's question asks for an o(k^2) bound on ch(G^2) in terms of chi(G^2), while Behzad's conjecture bounds the chromatic number (not choosability) of total graphs by Delta+2. Neither statement's truth forces the other's.

The source page explicitly says these questions 'are also related to the so-called List Total Colouring Conjecture'. Both descend from the disproved List Square Colouring Conjecture ch(G^2)=chi(G^2): LTCC is its special case on squares of subdivisions (total graphs), Noel's question is a weakened o(k^2)-bound version for all graphs. No implication either way: a positive answer to Noel's question allows a superlinear gap, far weaker than the exact equality LTCC demands on total graphs; and LTCC, restricted to total graphs, cannot bound ch(G^2) for general G. Explicitly stated relatedness, no derivable implication: related_only.

Steffen's source paper states explicitly: "Tutte's 3-flow conjecture is equivalent to the statement that Fc(G) <= 3 for every 5-graph G." The t=2 instance of the source conjecture is exactly that statement (2+2/t = 3, 5-graphs). Since the source conjecture asserts the bound for ALL t>1, its truth contains the t=2 case, which is equivalent to (hence implies) the 3-flow conjecture. The converse fails: the 3-flow conjecture says nothing about t>2. So the relation is a strict one-way implication, not equivalence, matching the OPG context "For t=2 it is Tutte's 3-flow conjecture." (Note the source is now disproved for large even t, but the t=2 case and thus the implication route remain intact.)

Explicit in the OPG context (written by Steffen): truth for even t implies Jaeger's conjecture for (4t'+1)-regular graphs and hence, by a result of Jaeger, the 5-flow conjecture. Self-contained check via t=4: the 5-flow conjecture reduces to 3-edge-connected cubic graphs G. Tripling every edge gives a 9-regular graph 3G whose cuts are 3x those of G, hence >= 9, so 3G is a 9-graph. Fc(3G) <= 2+2/4 = 5/2 is equivalent to a mod-5 orientation of 3G; the net contribution of each parallel triple (three +-1's) to the corresponding edge of G lies in {+-1,+-3}, never 0 mod 5, giving a nowhere-zero Z5-flow on G. Jaeger's reduction (9-edge-connected circular 5/2-flows imply the 5-flow conjecture) is documented in arXiv:1812.09833.

What is explicitly established (Steffen, arXiv:1310.8441 and the OPG context) is only: truth for even t=2t' implies Jaeger's conjecture restricted to (4t'+1)-REGULAR graphs (a 4t'-edge-connected (4t'+1)-regular graph is a (4t'+1)-graph, since its odd cuts are odd hence >= 4t'+1). The target as stated covers all 4k-edge-connected graphs, so the full implication needs the reduction of Jaeger's conjecture to its regular restriction. That equivalence is documented for k=1 (both equal the 3-flow conjecture) and is treated as folklore for general k (papers state Jaeger's conjecture in the regular form; the Han-Li-Wu-Zhang counterexamples are (4p+1)-regular and disprove both statements simultaneously), but I found no explicit general-k equivalence proof, so I stop short of confirming the full implication.

DIRECTION FLIPPED from the seed edge (which listed CDC as source). The Decomposing-Eulerian-graphs page states explicitly: "the above conjecture would imply the cycle double cover conjecture", and gives the argument: CDC reduces to 3-edge-connected graphs; replacing each edge of such a G by two parallel edges yields a 6-edge-connected Eulerian graph G' with the 2-transition system P pairing the parallel copies at each endpoint; a compatible decomposition of (G',P) uses at most one copy of each parallel pair per cycle, so projecting back to G gives a list of cycles covering every edge exactly twice, i.e., a CDC. The converse is not claimed anywhere, so this is a one-way implication: Decomposing Eulerian graphs is the stronger statement.

The CDC page only says 'Note the similarity between this conjecture and the Berge-Fulkerson conjecture' - an explicit analogy, not an implication. No implication is known in either direction: BF gives (via complements of the 6 matchings) six 2-factors covering each edge exactly 4 times, i.e. a cycle FOUR cover, which is already a theorem (Bermond-Jackson-Jaeger) and does not yield a double cover; conversely CDC says nothing about perfect matchings of cubic graphs. Both are known consequences of the common strengthening (Petersen coloring conjecture), which makes them thematically linked siblings, not logically comparable.

The truncated mention is misleading: fetching the full CDC page shows 'the above conjecture would follow from The three 4-flows conjecture' refers to the ORIENTED CYCLE FOUR COVER conjecture, a separate weaker statement hosted on the same page, not the CDC node's statement. The three 4-flows page confirms: 'it implies the Orientable cycle four cover conjecture' (each edge lies in exactly two of the graphs G\A_i, each having an orientable CDC via its nowhere-zero 4-flow, summing to a 4-cover). A cycle four cover does not give a double cover, and no implication between three 4-flows and CDC proper is known in either direction; both reduce to non-3-edge-colorable cubic graphs and both follow from Petersen coloring, but that makes them related family members only.

The mention is purely definitional: the source page says 'We insist on the usual restrictions for drawings (as in The Crossing Number of the Complete Graph)', importing the standard good-drawing conditions and nothing more. There is no logical dependence: the truth of the exact formula for cr(K_n) in the plane neither forces nor follows from the statement that optimal drawings of a disconnected graph on an arbitrary surface keep the components disjoint (the latter is about arbitrary graphs G_1, G_2 and arbitrary surfaces, the former about one specific family in the plane). They share only the theme of crossing-minimal drawings.

The OPG page explicitly says only 'Note the similarity of this to The Berge-Fulkerson conjecture' — a thematic comparison, not an implication. No implication holds via the obvious route: Berge-Fulkerson is equivalent (by complementing the 6 perfect matchings into 2-factors) to covering a cubic graph by six 2-factors using each edge exactly 4 times, but a faithful cover of (G,4) imposes neither the 2-factor structure nor the count of six cycles; indeed Bermond-Jackson-Jaeger already proved every bridgeless graph has a cycle cover using each edge exactly 4 times, yet Berge-Fulkerson remains open. Conversely Berge-Fulkerson concerns perfect matchings of cubic graphs and says nothing about general even admissible weightings. Companion conjectures with no known implication either way: related_only.

Dual notions in disjoint settings with no logical link. Friendly partitions (DeVos) asks whether all but finitely many finite r-regular graphs admit a partition where every vertex has at least as many neighbours in its own class; the unfriendly-partition problem (Cowan-Emerson) asks whether every countably infinite graph has a partition where every vertex has at least as many neighbours in the other class. The source page mentions unfriendly partitions only as contrast/motivation ('every finite graph has an unfriendly partition ... finding friendly partitions appears to be considerably more difficult'). One statement is about finite regular graphs with the 'friendly' inequality, the other about countably infinite graphs with the opposite inequality; truth of either has no bearing on the other. Thematically linked, no implication: related_only.

The source context compares Grunbaum's conjecture with the ORIENTABLE cycle double cover conjecture, and explicitly as a contrast, not an implication: Grunbaum's says every orientable embedding of a snark has a dual loop or parallel edge, while OCDC says some orientable embedding of every snark has no dual loop — near-opposite assertions about the same objects, neither implying the other. The target here is moreover the plain CDC, one step further removed (OCDC implies CDC, but Grunbaum's conjecture implies neither). Grunbaum's conjecture is in fact disproved (Kochol 2009: snarks with polyhedral embeddings in orientable surfaces) while CDC stands open, consistent only with the absence of implication in the other direction too. Twin conjectures about embedding snarks in orientable surfaces: related_only.
citations: M. Kochol, Polyhedral embeddings of snarks in orientable surfaces, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 137 (2009), 1613-1619

edges.argument: Both conjectures concern the same object, since chi''(H) = chi(T(H)). But they assert logically independent things: LTCC says the list chromatic number of a total graph equals its chromatic number (choosability = colorability), while TCC bounds that chromatic number by Delta(H)+2. Truth of LTCC gives no bound on chi(T(H)), and truth of TCC says nothing about list colorings, so neither implies the other. The OPG context itself only says the problem 'is related to ... the Total Colouring Conjecture'. (Note: their conjunction would give chi_ell(T(H)) <= Delta+2, but separately no implication holds.)

The source statement (every bridgeless graph has a (5,2)-cycle cover) is exactly the 5-cycle-double-cover conjecture, the (5,2) entry of the OPG chart; Berge-Fulkerson is equivalent (via complementing the six perfect matchings by 2-factors, extended from cubic graphs) to the (6,4) entry of the same chart. So the mention is that both conjectures are different boxes of the same (m,n)-cycle-cover table, not that one implies the other. No implication between 5CDC and Berge-Fulkerson is known in either direction (even whether BF implies the ordinary CDC is open); a (5,2)-cover does not yield a (6,4)-cover by any simple combination, nor conversely. Hence: strongly thematically linked, no established implication.

The mention says Seymour's r-graph conjecture 'is also closely related to Rizzi's packing postman sets conjecture (see packing T-joins)'. The target page's headline conjecture is about general grafts ((2/3)k - c disjoint T-joins), which Seymour's conjecture (chi' <= r+1 for r-graphs) cannot imply: it concerns arbitrary grafts, not r-regular graphs with T=V. Even for Rizzi's r-graph subcase (r-2 disjoint T-joins), an (r+1)-edge-coloring yields matchings that need not be perfect, hence not T-joins, so no direct implication follows; the pages assert closeness 'in nature' only. Both live in the same circle of ideas (Goldberg, r-graphs, matching/T-join decompositions) without a proven implication either way.

Both OPG pages state the connection explicitly, but it is only a partial implication: Seymour's Second Neighbourhood Conjecture implies the Behzad-Chartrand-Wall / triangle case of Caccetta-Haggkvist (min in- and out-degree >= n/3 forces a directed cycle of length <= 3), via the standard argument that a vertex with second outneighbourhood at least as large as its outneighbourhood in a triangle-free digraph would force more than n vertices. SSNC does not imply the full Caccetta-Haggkvist conjecture (general r, cycles of length ceil(n/r)), so 'implies' would overstate it; the correct classification is a well-documented partial-implication link, i.e. related_only.

The OPG context explicitly states only a case-level equivalence: the d=1 case of the splitting problem (Thomassen's f(1)=3) is equivalent to the k=2 case of Bermond-Thomassen (min outdegree 3 gives 2 disjoint cycles); indeed a bipartition with both parts of min outdegree >=1 yields two disjoint cycles, and conversely per Thomassen. But the full statements do not imply each other: for general d, splitting into two parts of min outdegree d says nothing about packing k disjoint cycles under the specific 2k-1 bound, and k disjoint cycles do not yield an outdegree-preserving bipartition. The problems are thematically linked with one coinciding special case, so related_only.

The mention is a methodological analogy only: 'As with the 5-flow conjecture or the cycle double cover conjecture, establishing this conjecture comes down to proving it for cubic graphs which are not 3-edge-colorable.' No implication is stated or derivable. Combining the 4-flows on G\A1 and G\A2 (which cover all of E(G) since A1,A2 are disjoint) yields only a nowhere-zero Z4xZ4-flow, i.e. a 16-flow, weaker than Seymour's unconditional 6-flow theorem, so the three-4-flows conjecture does not yield a 5-flow; conversely a nowhere-zero 5-flow gives no decomposition into three sets whose complements carry 4-flows. Both reduce to snarks and share the flow framework, so related_only.

Conclusion-wise the Pentagon problem is stronger: a homomorphism G -> C5 induces a cut-continuous mapping G -> C5, which is exactly the Weak pentagon conclusion (equivalently, edge 5-coloring with bipartite color-class complements / homomorphism to the Clebsch graph); the OPG text calls the weak conjecture 'a weaker version' for this reason. But the hypothesis classes are not nested in the required direction: Pentagon assumes girth at least g for sufficiently large g, while Weak pentagon covers ALL triangle-free (girth >= 4) cubic graphs. A positive Pentagon answer would establish the weak conclusion only for high-girth graphs, leaving girths 4..g-1 unsettled, so the full statements do not stand in an implication; the connection is instance-wise on a subfamily. Hence related_only (Pentagon truth would settle the high-girth part and be strong evidence).

Halin's conjecture is about infinite graphs; the Reconstruction Conjecture is about finite graphs with at least 3 vertices. Their hypothesis classes do not overlap, so neither statement implies the other. The link itself is real: bm-003's context says Halin's conjecture is the natural weakening, for infinite graphs, of the finite Reconstruction Conjecture (hypomorphic implies isomorphic), which fails for infinite graphs. Halin's conjecture being disproved has no bearing on the finite problem.

Direction reversed from the seed: the refinement implies Barát–Thomassen. Assume the refinement holds with function f. For a tree T, set k(T) = max(f(Delta_T), f(|E(T)|)). A k-edge-connected graph is f(Delta_T)-edge-connected and has minimum degree at least k >= f(|E(T)|). So when e(G) is divisible by e(T), G is T-decomposable, and this holds for simple graphs in particular. That is exactly Barát–Thomassen. The refinement's own context calls it a refinement of Conjecture 1.1 (Barát–Thomassen). The implication is valid as a logical relation even though the refinement is recorded as disproved and Barát–Thomassen as solved.

A cycle double cover with at most n-1 cycles is, in particular, a cycle double cover, so Bondy's conjecture gives CDC for simple bridgeless graphs. CDC for general bridgeless graphs reduces to the simple case by standard steps. A loop is a cycle and can be used twice. Degree-2 vertices can be suppressed, and vertex splitting reduces the problem to simple cubic (indeed 3-connected cubic) graphs, as the target's own context notes. bm-013's context also says it explicitly: 'This strengthens the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture'.

Direction: the strong form implies the plain form. Every bridgeless cubic graph contains a circuit, so the strong 5-CDC conjecture yields a double cover of every bridgeless cubic graph by five 2-regular subgraphs. In a cubic graph these are exactly the nonempty even subgraphs. The general 5-CDC conjecture reduces to bridgeless cubic graphs by the standard steps: suppress degree-2 vertices, split higher-degree vertices while keeping 2-edge-connectivity (Fleischner's splitting lemma), and pull the even-subgraph covers back. The target's context states explicitly that it strengthens the 5-cycle double cover conjecture.

Each even subgraph is an edge-disjoint union of cycles. Take a double cover by at most five even subgraphs and decompose each subgraph into its cycles. The resulting list of cycles covers every edge exactly twice, which is a CDC. A 2-edge-connected graph and a bridgeless graph are the same notion here: for disconnected graphs, apply the conjecture to each component. The target's context also lists the 5-CDC conjecture as a strengthening of CDC.

Direction: the Petersen coloring conjecture implies 5-CDC. The target node's own context says so explicitly ('would imply both Berge–Fulkerson and the five cycle double cover conjecture'). Proof sketch: the Petersen graph P has a double cover by five even subgraphs. A Petersen coloring (a cycle-continuous map G -> P) pulls each of these back to an even subgraph of G, and each edge of G still lies in exactly two of them. This proves 5-CDC for bridgeless cubic graphs, and the standard reduction extends it to all bridgeless graphs. The equivalent form stated in the context, a cycle-continuous map from every bridgeless graph, covers general graphs directly.

The target defines a binary cycle as an edge set in which every vertex has even degree, which is an even subgraph. A (5,2)-cycle-cover is a list of 5 such sets covering each edge exactly twice. 'At most five' and 'exactly five' coincide because the empty set is a binary cycle and can pad the list. The bridgeless and 2-edge-connected hypotheses match componentwise. So the node's stated conjecture 'every bridgeless graph has a (5,2)-cycle-cover' is literally the 5-CDC conjecture; the page's chart even labels the (5,2) entry '5CDC conj'. The page also discusses a wider (m,n) framework, but the stated conjecture is the same statement.

For odd Delta, the LAC bound is ceil((Delta+1)/2) = (Delta+1)/2 linear forests. The target's partition into (Delta-1)/2 linear forests plus one matching is at least that strong, because a matching is a linear forest. So the arXiv conjecture implies LAC only for planar graphs of odd Delta >= 7, not LAC in general, and LAC does not give the matching refinement. Also, LAC is already known for planar graphs. The node's own context calls it a refinement of the planar linear arboricity bound, so the link is real, but neither statement implies the other.

bm-021 asks about the complexity of finding a second Hamilton cycle in cubic graphs, where the cycle is known to exist by Smith's theorem. The target claims a second Hamilton cycle exists in 4-connected graphs. Cubic graphs are never 4-connected, so the two hypothesis classes are disjoint, and an existence claim cannot settle a complexity question or the reverse. The only link is thematic (both concern uniquely hamiltonian graphs and second Hamilton cycles), so this is related_only at most.

The target's r=3 case is Smith's theorem, which bm-021's context cites as the reason a second Hamilton cycle always exists in cubic graphs. Thomason proved it for all odd r. bm-021 asks whether that cycle can be found in polynomial time, which is a complexity question that neither implies nor is implied by the existence statement for other r. The dependency is documented but it is not an implication.

The plain circular embedding conjecture gives a cycle double cover by face boundaries, but that cover is neither orientable nor limited to 5 even subgraphs, so it does not imply bm-026. Conversely, an orientable 5-even-subgraph double cover does not give a surface embedding whose faces are all cycles, because pinch points can occur for non-cubic graphs. The target's context names two strengthenings, one with a 5-colourable dual and one orientable, which imply the 5-CDC and the oriented CDC respectively. Only a combined orientable strengthening with a 5-colourable dual would imply bm-026, and that combined form is not the target node's statement.

2-edge-connected is the same as having no bridge. Each even subgraph in a double cover decomposes into edge-disjoint cycles. So an (orientable) double cover by five even subgraphs yields a list of cycles in which every edge appears exactly twice, which is the CDC. bm-026's context also says it strengthens the 5-CDC, which itself implies the CDC.

Grünbaum's conjecture (disproved by Kochol) says embeddings of snarks in orientable surfaces must have a dual with a loop or parallel edges. The OPG context contrasts it with the orientable CDC, which bm-026 strengthens. Neither statement implies the other: one is about duals of simple triangulations, the other about even-subgraph covers. The connection is indirect, running through the orientable CDC rather than bm-026 itself, so it is only a documented thematic relation.

Both statements imply the orientable cycle 4-cover conjecture. For bm-026, take the orientable double cover twice. For the three 4-flows conjecture, each G\A_i has an orientable CDC because it has a nowhere-zero 4-flow, and every edge lies in exactly two of the G\A_i. So they share a consequence. I know of no reduction in either direction between an orientable 5-even-subgraph double cover and a 3-part decomposition into 4-flow complements, so the relation is related_only.

The target's own context discusses the even-cycle family case: the Turán number of a family of even cycles should be governed (up to constants) by its longest cycle. Neither statement implies the other. bm-034 is a lower bound for one forbidden cycle. The family conjecture only compares ex(n,F) with ex(n,family), so it gives no lower bound of order n^{1+1/k}. Conversely, a lower bound for ex(n,C_{2k}) says nothing about arbitrary finite families. The link is real, but it is not an implication.

The target's context presents List Hadwiger as the list-colouring analogue of Hadwiger's conjecture. Hadwiger does not imply it, because list chromatic number can exceed chromatic number; Voigt's example shows that K_5-minor-free graphs need not be 4-list-colourable. List Hadwiger does not imply Hadwiger either, because a ct-list-colouring with c>=1 (and c>=4/3 is necessary by Barát–Joret–Wood) is weaker than a (t-1)-colouring. So the two are related, but neither implies the other.

Hadwiger's conjecture is equivalent to chi(G) <= had(G) for all G. The standard inequalities are chi_f <= chi and had <= had_f. Hadwiger therefore gives (a) chi_f <= chi <= had, (b) chi <= had <= had_f, and (c) chi_f <= had_f. The target's context says explicitly that these conjectures are weaker than Hadwiger's conjecture.

Take an n-vertex graph with independence number at most 2. Every colour class has at most 2 vertices, so chi >= n/2, and Hadwiger then gives a K_{ceil(n/2)} minor. The target's own context proves this implication and calls the Seagull problem an unproved consequence of Hadwiger's conjecture.

The target (Abu-Khzam–Langston) is the immersion analogue of Hadwiger's conjecture, and its context explicitly compares it with Hadwiger's and Hajós' conjectures. Minor containment and immersion containment are incomparable in general: a K_t minor does not yield a K_t immersion, and a K_t immersion does not yield a K_t minor. So neither conjecture implies the other. The connection is documented, but there is no implication.

The target's context names Hadwiger's conjecture as motivation. The Robertson–Seymour–Thomas proof for K_6-minor-free graphs shows that a minimal counterexample is apex, which comes close to Jørgensen's statement. Still, Jørgensen's conjecture is a structural claim about 6-connected K_6-minor-free graphs. It does not follow from any colouring statement, and it does not imply Hadwiger for general k. So they are related, but neither implies the other.

A subdivision of K_t yields an immersion of K_t: its branch paths are edge-disjoint and can be split off into edges. So Hajós' conjecture at k=t implies the immersion conjecture at t. However, bm-042 asks only about k=5,6. It would give only the t=5,6 cases of the target, which the target's context says are already proved (DeVos–Kawarabayashi–Mohar–Okamura, t<=7). There is therefore no implication to the full all-t conjecture, only a documented analogy (the target's context names Hajós explicitly).

Let G be a connected double-critical k-chromatic graph. For any vertex v with a neighbour u, chi(G-v) <= chi(G-u-v)+1 = k-1, so G is vertex-critical. A vertex-critical k-chromatic graph that contains K_k equals K_k, so if G is not K_k then it has no k-clique. Apply Erdős–Lovász Tihany with k1=2, k2=k-1: we get disjoint G1 (2-chromatic, so it contains an edge xy) and G2 with chi = k-1 lying inside G-x-y. This contradicts chi(G-x-y)=k-2. So the k1=2 case of the source implies the target, and the target's context says it is a special case of the Erdős–Lovász problem.

The direction is reversed from the seed: Gyárfás–Sumner implies the triangle-free tree statement. If a triangle-free graph G omitted some finite tree T as an induced subgraph, then every finite subgraph of G would be triangle-free and T-free. It would therefore have chromatic number at most f_T(2). By de Bruijn–Erdős compactness, chi(G) <= f_T(2) is finite, a contradiction. The source node's context states this derivation explicitly. The converse (from omega=2 to all omega) is not a known reduction, so the relation is implies, not equivalent_to.

The unit-distance graph is a spanning subgraph of the odd-distance graph, so chi(R^2) <= chi(O). This gives only an inequality between the two unknowns; neither open question settles the other. Determining chi(R^2) (known to lie in 5..7) says nothing about whether chi(O) is infinite, and chi(O) = infinity says nothing about chi(R^2). The target's context explicitly calls the question a relative of the unit-distance colouring problem. So the link is documented but there is no implication.

Both are Gallai-type questions about the intersection of longest cycles and paths, and they are treated side by side in that literature (e.g. the Shabbir–Zamfirescu–Zamfirescu survey on intersecting longest paths and cycles; not fetched here). Neither implies the other. One is about pairs of longest cycles in k-connected graphs meeting in >= k vertices; the other is about triples of longest paths in connected graphs sharing one vertex. The connection is real as an analogy but was not verified by a citation I fetched, hence plausible.

Birmelé's conjecture is the sharp n=2 case (hitting-set bound exactly k) of the undirected Erdős–Pósa property for cycles of length >= k. The target is the directed analogue with an unspecified bound t_n(l). Replacing each edge by two opposite arcs (for l >= 3) shows the directed statement gives an undirected Erdős–Pósa bound, but only some t_2, not the sharp value k. So the target does not imply the source, and the source (undirected) does not imply the directed statement. The target's context cites the Birmelé–Bondy–Reed undirected result, which makes the thematic link real, but there is no implication.

The OPG context for Caccetta-Häggkvist explicitly calls the Bollobás-Scott statement a 'weighted version' and discusses it, so the link is documented. Neither implies the other. The weighted statement asks for a LONG cycle (weight >= 1). With uniform weights 1/r it only gives a cycle of length >= r, which is the easy long-cycle fact, not a short cycle of length <= ceil(n/r). Conversely, CH says nothing about weighted long cycles. The hypotheses also differ: BM requires strong connectivity and positive weights, while the OPG version uses weights in [0,1].

Line graphs are claw-free, so Matthews-Sumner implies Thomassen's conjecture by hypothesis-class containment. For the converse, Ryjáček's closure cl(G) of a claw-free graph G is the line graph of a triangle-free graph. It keeps connectivity (it only adds edges) and preserves the circumference, so G is Hamiltonian iff cl(G) is (Ryjáček, JCTB 70 (1997)). Hence Thomassen's conjecture implies Matthews-Sumner. Both nodes' contexts state this equivalence explicitly.

Thomassen's conjecture allows finitely many non-Hamiltonian connected vertex-transitive graphs. Nothing forces these exceptions to have Hamiltonian paths, so it does not imply Lovász's 'every connected VT graph has a Hamiltonian path'. Conversely, having a Hamiltonian path does not give Hamiltonian cycles in all but finitely many cases. The OPG context documents the connection explicitly: it lists the same five known non-Hamiltonian VT graphs and the same Hamiltonian-cycle question.

Connected Cayley graphs are vertex-transitive, so Thomassen's conjecture gives 'all but finitely many connected Cayley graphs are Hamiltonian'. That is weaker than the question 'is every Cayley graph Hamiltonian?', since finitely many Cayley exceptions are not ruled out (K2 = Cay(Z2) is already a degenerate one). So there is no implication in either direction. The link is documented: the OPG context cites the vertex-transitive generalisation, and the BM sketch calls Cayley graphs a special case.

Given f from the source conjecture and a tree T with m leaves, set k(T) = max(f(m), f(e(T))). A k(T)-edge-connected graph is f(m)-edge-connected, because edge-connectivity thresholds are monotone. It also has minimum degree >= k(T) >= f(e(T)), since min degree >= edge-connectivity. If e(G) is divisible by e(T), the source then gives a T-decomposition. The target's restriction to simple graphs only shrinks the class. This is exactly Barát-Thomassen. (The target is also already proved, so the implication holds trivially as well.)

An orientable double cover by five even subgraphs is, after forgetting the orientations, a double cover by at most five even subgraphs, and both statements have the same hypothesis (2-edge-connected graphs). So the orientable version implies the plain 5-CDC. The source node's context says explicitly that it strengthens the five cycle double cover conjecture.

Let T be a tree on n>=2 vertices, so k=n-1 edges. In a 2-colouring of K_N with N=2n-2, one colour class has at least (n-1)(2n-3)/2 edges, and (n-1)(2n-3)/2 > (n-1)(n-2) = N(k-1)/2 because n-3/2 > n-2. Erdős–Sós then says that colour class contains every tree with k edges, T included, so r(T,T) <= 2n-2. This is the standard remark that Erdős–Sós implies the Burr–Erdős tree Ramsey bound.

Hadwiger's conjecture is equivalent to: every K_{t+1}-minor-free graph has chi <= t (if chi >= t+1, then some (t+1)-chromatic subgraph would have a K_{t+1} minor). A proper t-colouring of an n-vertex graph has a colour class of size >= n/t, so alpha(G) >= n/t. The target node's own context states exactly this implication.

A subdivision of K_t has crossing number >= cr(K_t), so Hajós for a given k implies Albertson's conjecture for t=k. The source covers only k=5,6, so at most it yields Albertson for t=5,6, which is already known (Albertson's conjecture is known for t <= 16). It gives nothing for general t. In the other direction, Albertson does not force a topological K_k. The target's context documents the link: it calls Albertson's conjecture a weakening of Hajós's conjecture. So the connection is real, but it is not an implication between these nodes.

A K_k-subdivision is a K_k-minor, so Hajós for k implies Hadwiger for the same k. The source node covers only k=5,6, and those cases of Hadwiger are already theorems (Wagner + 4CT; Robertson–Seymour–Thomas). So the source does not imply the general Hadwiger node. Hadwiger also does not imply the existence of subdivisions. The relation is related_only: specialization at shared values of k.

In the hypergraph game, players move along hyperedges instead of edges. A connected 2-uniform hypergraph is a connected graph, and there the game is the usual Cops and Robbers game. The conjectured bound c(H)=O(sqrt(n/k)) uses an absolute implied constant. At k=2 it gives c(G) <= C sqrt(n/2) = O(sqrt n) for every connected graph, which is Meyniel's conjecture. The paper itself presents its conjecture as a generalization of Meyniel's.

The Matthews–Sumner conjecture is known to be equivalent (Ryjáček closure; Fleischner–Jackson 1989; Kochol) to Thomassen's conjecture and to Fleischner's dominating cycle conjecture: every cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph has a dominating cycle C, meaning every edge has an end on C. Given such a C in a cubic graph, the vertices off C form an independent set, and each of them has all 3 of its neighbours on C. Each vertex of C has 2 cycle-neighbours, so at most one neighbour off C. Counting edges between C and V-C gives 3(n-|C|) <= |C|, so |C| >= 3n/4, which proves Bondy's conjecture with c=3/4. The converse does not follow.

By Steinitz, a 3-connected cubic planar graph G is the graph of a simple 3-polytope P. P x [0,1] is a simple 4-polytope, and its graph is G□K_2. So Barnette's 4-polytope conjecture, restricted to prisms, says G□K_2 is Hamiltonian. The Hamilton-decomposition conjecture also implies that statement. That shared special case is already a theorem (Rosenfeld–Barnette via 4CT, cited in the target's context). Barnette gives only one Hamilton cycle, not a decomposition. The target covers only prisms, not all simple 4-polytopes. So neither node implies the other.

Oum (arXiv:2607.16356v3, Sec. 9.3) states Conjecture 21 (Archdeacon; Jaeger: every bridgeless graph has an orientable 5-CDC, i.e. at most 5 Eulerian=even subgraphs, each with an Eulerian orientation, every edge used once in each direction), remarks it implies Tutte's 5-flow conjecture, and proves Lemma 22 (= Lemma 13.1.5 in Zhang's book): an orientable k-CDC gives a nowhere-zero Z_k-flow. Proof re-derived: pad to exactly k subgraphs C_1..C_k (so 'at most five' vs 'exactly five' is immaterial), fix a reference orientation, let chi_i be the signed characteristic vector of the directed Eulerian C_i (an integer circulation), and set phi = sum_i i*chi_i mod k. Each edge e lies in exactly two distinct C_i, C_j (an even subgraph contains an edge at most once) traversed in opposite directions, so phi(e) = ±(i-j) with 1 <= |i-j| <= 4, nonzero mod 5. Tutte's theorem (Z_k-flow iff integer k-flow) turns this into a nowhere-zero 5-flow. The BM hypothesis ('2-edge-connected') vs the target ('bridgeless') is bridged by working componentwise (flows are local to components; loops take any nonzero value and can be removed first), so the node statement exactly matches the lemma's hypothesis.
citations: arXiv:2607.16356v3 (S. Oum, A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: an exposition), Section 9.3, Conjecture 21 and Lemma 22
C.-Q. Zhang, Integer Flows and Cycle Covers of Graphs, Lemma 13.1.5 (cited by Oum; not read directly)
